title: WEBSEC 15 - Cross-site scripting (XSS) part 1: Reflected, stored and DOM-based

questions.q: Cross-site scripting lets an attacker get around which browser security mechanism, the one meant to keep different websites apart?
choices: The same origin policy
The Content-Type header
TLS certificate validation
HTTP basic authentication
questions.explain: XSS lets an attacker get around the same origin policy, which is meant to keep different websites apart. The injected script runs as if it were part of the vulnerable site.

questions.q: In general, how does cross-site scripting work?
choices: It manipulates a vulnerable website so that it returns malicious JavaScript to users, and that code runs in the victim's browser
It injects SQL into a database query to read server-side tables
It tricks a victim into sending an unintended state-changing request without running any script
It intercepts traffic between the browser and the server on the network
questions.explain: XSS makes the site return attacker-controlled JavaScript. When that code runs in the victim's browser, the attacker can fully compromise the victim's interaction with the application.

questions.q: Of the three main XSS types, which one is described as 'the malicious script comes from the website's database'?
choices: Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
DOM-based XSS
Self-XSS
questions.explain: In reflected XSS the script comes from the current HTTP request. In stored XSS it comes from the website's database. In DOM-based XSS the flaw is in client-side code, not server-side code.

questions.q: What is the difference between XSS and SQL injection?
choices: XSS is a client-side vulnerability that targets other application users; SQL injection is a server-side vulnerability that targets the application's database
XSS targets the database; SQL injection targets other users' browsers
They are the same vulnerability with different payload syntax
XSS only affects administrators; SQL injection only affects anonymous users
questions.explain: XSS attacks other users through their browsers (client side). SQL injection attacks the application's database (server side).

questions.q: What is the difference between XSS and CSRF?
choices: XSS makes a website return malicious JavaScript; CSRF induces a victim to perform actions they do not intend
CSRF makes a website return malicious JavaScript; XSS induces a victim to perform unintended actions
XSS works only over HTTP; CSRF works only over HTTPS
There is no difference; CSRF is another name for stored XSS
questions.explain: XSS gets the site to return malicious JavaScript. CSRF tricks the victim's browser into making requests the user did not intend.

questions.q: In which situation will a successful XSS attack generally have CRITICAL impact?
choices: The compromised user has elevated privileges within the application
The application is brochureware where all users are anonymous and all information is public
The vulnerable page is only reachable over HTTPS
The application has no login functionality at all
questions.explain: If the victim has elevated privileges, the attacker may take full control of the application and compromise all users and their data. In anonymous, all-public brochureware the impact is often minimal. Apps holding sensitive data (banking, email, healthcare) usually suffer serious impact.

questions.q: Which of the following can an attacker typically do by exploiting an XSS vulnerability?
choices: Impersonate the victim user
Carry out any action the user is able to perform
Capture the user's login credentials
Perform virtual defacement of the website
Directly read files from the web server's filesystem
questions.explain: XSS runs in the victim's browser with the victim's session. It allows impersonation, any action the user can perform, reading the user's data, stealing credentials, virtual defacement, and injecting trojan functionality. It does not give direct access to the server's filesystem.

questions.q: From Chrome 92 onward, cross-origin iframes cannot call alert(). Which harmless JavaScript function is recommended instead as a proof-of-concept that script execution happened?
questions.explain: Since Chrome 92 (July 2021), cross-origin iframes can't call alert(), so print() is the recommended alternative proof of concept.

questions.q: XSS vulnerabilities are very common, and XSS is probably the most frequently occurring web security vulnerability.
questions.explain: XSS vulnerabilities are very common, although reliable data on real-world XSS attacks is hard to get.

questions.q: Reflected XSS arises when an application...
choices: receives data in an HTTP request and includes that data within the immediate response in an unsafe way
stores untrusted data and includes it in later HTTP responses in an unsafe way
has client-side JavaScript that writes untrusted data back to the DOM
reflects data only when the victim pastes it into their own browser console
questions.explain: Reflected = request data echoed unsafely in the immediate response. Stored = saved and echoed in later responses. DOM-based = client-side JS processing untrusted data unsafely.

questions.q: Why is reflected XSS generally less severe than stored XSS?
choices: It needs an external delivery mechanism to get the victim to make the attacker's request
Reflected payloads can never access the victim's session
Browsers automatically block all reflected scripts
Reflected XSS can only affect the attacker's own account
questions.explain: With reflected XSS the attacker must get the victim to make a crafted request, for example through a link in an email or on another site. Stored XSS is self-contained inside the vulnerable application.

questions.q: Which are ways an attacker might get a victim to make the request needed for a reflected XSS attack?
choices: Placing a link on a website the attacker controls
Placing a link on another website that allows user-generated content
Sending a link in an email, tweet or other message
Waiting for the victim to browse to a blog comment stored in the vulnerable app
questions.explain: Reflected XSS is delivered through links on attacker-controlled sites, on sites with user-generated content, or in messages. A payload waiting inside the application describes stored XSS.

questions.q: Once a reflected XSS attack runs, which of these can the attacker typically do as the victim?
choices: View any information the user is able to view
Modify any information the user is able to modify
Initiate interactions with other application users that appear to come from the victim
Gain operating-system access on the victim's machine
questions.explain: A script the attacker controls in the victim's browser can do anything the user can do in the application, including interacting with other users as the victim. OS-level access is not part of XSS impact.

questions.q: What is self-XSS?
choices: Behavior like reflected XSS that cannot be triggered through a crafted URL or cross-domain request, only by the victim submitting the payload themselves
Stored XSS where the attacker is also the only victim
DOM XSS that only fires on the attacker's own machine
XSS that exploits the browser's own internal pages
questions.explain: Self-XSS can only be triggered by the victim submitting the payload from their own browser, which usually requires social engineering. It is normally considered a low-impact issue.

questions.q: For reflected XSS, where the data appears in the response, plus any validation the app applies to it, affects what kind of payload is needed.
questions.explain: The reflection context (between tags, inside a quoted attribute, inside a JavaScript string, and so on) and any processing or validation determine what payload is needed and can affect impact.

questions.q: Stored XSS is also known by two other names. Give one.
questions.explain: Stored XSS is also called persistent XSS or second-order XSS.

questions.q: Stored XSS arises when an application...
choices: receives data from an untrusted source and includes that data within its later HTTP responses in an unsafe way
includes request data only in the immediate response
only processes data in client-side JavaScript
rejects all user input containing angle brackets
questions.explain: In stored XSS the untrusted data is saved and then appears unsafely in later responses, which may be served to other users.

questions.q: Which are examples of untrusted data sources that could lead to stored XSS?
choices: Comments on a blog post
A webmail application displaying messages received over SMTP
A marketing application displaying social media posts
A network monitoring application displaying packet data
A hard-coded string constant in the server's source code
questions.explain: Stored data can come from HTTP requests (comments, nicknames, contact details) or out-of-band sources (email, social media posts, network traffic). A hard-coded developer constant is not attacker-controlled.

questions.q: Suppose an XSS vulnerability only affects logged-in users. Why does stored XSS have an advantage over reflected XSS here?
choices: Users who come across the stored exploit inside the application are guaranteed to be logged in, so the attack doesn't depend on lucky timing
Stored XSS can force users to log in
Reflected XSS cannot run while users are logged in
Stored XSS bypasses the need for a session altogether
questions.explain: A reflected attack only works if the victim happens to be logged in when they make the attacker's request. A stored exploit sits inside the app, so anyone who reaches it is logged in.

questions.q: The exit points for stored XSS are limited to the responses returned to the user who originally submitted the data.
questions.explain: Exit points are all possible HTTP responses returned to any kind of application user in any situation. For example, a display name might show up in an obscure audit log that only some users can see.

questions.q: Why is mapping the links between entry points and exit points challenging when testing for stored XSS?
choices: Data submitted at any entry point could, in principle, come out at any exit point
Stored data is often overwritten by other actions in the application (e.g., a recent-searches list)
Testing every entry/exit permutation separately is impractical in an application with more than a few pages
Stored data never appears in HTTP responses
questions.explain: Data can surface anywhere, stored values can be replaced quickly, and exhaustive permutation testing is impractical. Instead, testers work through entry points systematically and watch the responses.

questions.q: During stored XSS testing, your submitted value shows up in a response. What must you determine next?
choices: Whether the data is actually stored across different requests, rather than just reflected in the immediate response
Whether the server is running PHP
Whether the value appears in the browser's address bar
Whether the response used HTTP/2
questions.explain: Seeing the value in the response isn't enough. You must confirm it persists across requests, which makes it stored rather than just reflected.

questions.q: Which are entry points to consider for stored XSS?
choices: Parameters in the URL query string and message body
The URL file path
HTTP request headers that might not be exploitable for reflected XSS
Out-of-band routes such as incoming emails or third-party feeds
questions.explain: All four are entry points. Headers that are useless for reflected XSS can still matter for stored XSS, and out-of-band routes depend on what the application does.

questions.q: DOM-based XSS vulnerabilities usually arise when...
choices: JavaScript takes data from an attacker-controllable source and passes it to a sink that supports dynamic code execution
the server stores data in a database and outputs it later
the server reflects a query parameter into the HTML response without JavaScript involvement
a CSP header is missing
questions.explain: DOM XSS is a source-to-sink flow in client-side JavaScript. Examples are data from the URL reaching eval() or innerHTML.

questions.q: What is the most common source for DOM XSS?
choices: The URL, typically accessed through the window.location object
The server's database
The HTTP Content-Type response header
Local filesystem files
questions.explain: The URL (window.location) is the most common source. The query string and fragment are typical places for the data, and in some cases (404 pages, PHP sites) the path is too.

questions.q: Why doesn't the browser's 'View source' option work for DOM XSS testing?
choices: It shows the original HTML and ignores changes JavaScript made to the page
It is disabled on pages that use JavaScript
It only shows HTTP headers
It URL-decodes every value on the page
questions.explain: View source shows the HTML as the server sent it. DOM XSS involves changes made by JavaScript, so you inspect the live DOM with developer tools instead.

questions.q: Why is testing JavaScript execution sinks harder than testing HTML sinks for DOM XSS?
choices: Your input doesn't necessarily appear anywhere in the DOM, so you have to trace it with the JavaScript debugger
Execution sinks only exist in Internet Explorer
Execution sinks always URL-encode their input
Execution sinks cannot receive data from the URL
questions.explain: Input sent to execution sinks may never appear in the DOM. You find where the source is read in the code, set breakpoints, and follow the value (including through other variables) to the sink.

questions.q: Chrome, Firefox and Safari URL-encode location.search and location.hash, and if your data gets URL-encoded before being processed, an XSS attack is unlikely to work.
questions.explain: Modern Chrome, Firefox and Safari URL-encode these sources, which usually stops exploitation. IE11 and pre-Chromium Edge did not.

questions.q: Which of these are listed as main sinks that can lead to DOM-XSS vulnerabilities?
choices: document.write()
element.innerHTML
element.outerHTML
element.insertAdjacentHTML
element.textContent
Math.random()
questions.explain: The listed sinks include document.write(), document.writeln(), document.domain, element.innerHTML, element.outerHTML, element.insertAdjacentHTML and element.onevent. textContent and Math.random() are not on the list.

questions.q: On modern browsers, script elements inserted through innerHTML do not execute.
questions.explain: innerHTML doesn't accept script elements on any modern browser, and svg onload events won't fire either. That is why innerHTML sinks are usually exploited through other elements with event handlers.

questions.q: Older jQuery code often passed location.hash to the $() selector. How did newer jQuery versions mitigate this classic DOM XSS?
choices: They stop HTML from being injected into a selector when the input begins with a '#' character
They removed the $() function entirely
They made location.hash read-only
They automatically apply a Content Security Policy
questions.explain: Newer jQuery blocks HTML injection into selectors that start with '#'. The $() sink can still be vulnerable if the attacker fully controls input from a source that doesn't need a '#' prefix.

questions.q: On a page where an element has the ng-app attribute (AngularJS), why might HTML-encoding angle brackets not be enough to prevent XSS?
choices: AngularJS evaluates expressions inside double curly braces, in HTML or in attributes, so JavaScript can run without angle brackets or events
AngularJS automatically decodes all HTML entities into script tags
AngularJS disables the same origin policy
AngularJS turns every attribute into an event handler
questions.explain: AngularJS processes elements under ng-app and runs expressions inside {{ }}. Injection can work even when angle brackets are encoded.

questions.q: Which of these jQuery functions are listed as sinks that can lead to DOM-XSS?
choices: html()
append()
after()
$.parseHTML()
text()
val()
questions.explain: The listed jQuery sinks include add(), after(), append(), animate(), insertAfter(), insertBefore(), before(), html(), prepend(), replaceAll(), replaceWith(), wrap(), wrapInner(), wrapAll(), has(), constructor(), init(), index(), jQuery.parseHTML() and $.parseHTML(). text() and val() are not on the list.

questions.q: In a reflected DOM XSS vulnerability...
choices: the server echoes request data into the response (e.g., into a JavaScript string or form field), and a script on the page then writes it unsafely to a dangerous sink
the server stores data and a later page's script writes it to a sink
the data never reaches the server and stays only in the URL fragment
the victim pastes the payload into their own console
questions.explain: Reflected DOM XSS: the server reflects the data, then client-side script handles it unsafely. In stored DOM XSS the server stores the data and a script in a later response sends it to a sink.

questions.q: A pure DOM-based XSS vulnerability can be contained within a single page and be entirely client-side.
questions.explain: If a script reads data from the URL and writes it to a dangerous sink, the vulnerability is entirely client-side.

questions.q: When testing entry points for reflected XSS, about how many characters long is the ideal random alphanumeric test value?
questions.explain: About 8 characters is ideal. That is short enough to survive most input validation and long enough that accidental matches in the response are very unlikely.

questions.q: Why should the test value for finding reflections be short and contain only alphanumeric characters?
choices: So it survives most input validation, while still being long enough to avoid accidental matches in the response
So it executes as JavaScript right away
Because special characters are never reflected
So that it gets stored in the database
questions.explain: The aim at this stage is just to find where input is reflected. Plain alphanumeric values avoid triggering filters.

questions.q: Which entry points should be tested separately for reflected XSS?
choices: Parameters in the URL query string
Parameters in the message body
The URL file path
HTTP headers
questions.explain: All of these should be tested. XSS-like behavior that only certain HTTP headers can trigger may not be exploitable in practice.

questions.q: To find DOM-based vulnerabilities in non-URL-based input (like document.cookie) or non-HTML sinks (like setTimeout), what is described as having no substitute?
choices: Reviewing the JavaScript code
Searching the page with 'View source'
Checking the HTTP status codes
Submitting random values in HTTP headers
questions.explain: These cases need JavaScript code review, which can take a long time. Automated tools combine static and dynamic analysis of JavaScript to help.

questions.q: After finding where a test value is reflected, what is the next step before choosing a candidate payload?
choices: Determine the reflection context (text between tags, a quoted attribute, a JavaScript string, etc.)
Immediately test in a real browser
Report the vulnerability as confirmed
Switch to testing for SQL injection
questions.explain: The context decides which payload can work. After that, you test candidate payloads, try alternatives if they are filtered, and finally confirm in a real browser.

questions.q: Effective XSS prevention generally combines which measures?
choices: Filter input on arrival, as strictly as possible based on what is expected
Encode data on output so it isn't interpreted as active content
Use appropriate response headers
Content Security Policy as a last line of defense
Rely on the browser to block all injected scripts by default
questions.explain: Prevention combines strict input filtering, context-appropriate output encoding, correct response headers, and CSP as a last line of defense. Browsers do not block injected scripts by default.

questions.q: Which headers help prevent XSS in HTTP responses that aren't meant to contain any HTML or JavaScript?
choices: Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options
Cache-Control and Expires
Host and Referer
Accept-Language and Accept-Encoding
questions.explain: Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options make sure browsers interpret the response the way the developer intended.

questions.q: Depending on the output context, encoding data on output might require combining HTML, URL, JavaScript and CSS encoding.
questions.explain: Output encoding has to match the context where the data lands, and that can mean several encoding types together.

questions.q: Which statement about Content Security Policy (CSP) is accurate?
choices: It is a browser mechanism that can hinder or prevent XSS exploitation, but it can often be circumvented, so it works best as a last line of defense
It completely removes the need for output encoding
It is a server-side database filter
It only protects against SQL injection
questions.explain: CSP reduces the impact of XSS. It can often be bypassed, so it is a last line of defense and not a replacement for fixing the underlying flaw.

questions.q: What is dangling markup injection?
choices: A technique for capturing data cross-domain when a full XSS exploit isn't possible because of input filters or other defenses
A way of encoding output to prevent XSS
Another name for self-XSS
A CSP directive that blocks inline scripts
questions.explain: Dangling markup injection can capture sensitive information visible to other users, such as CSRF tokens, even when full script execution is blocked.

questions.q: In PHP, which approach is recommended for escaping output in HTML contexts?
choices: htmlentities with ENT_QUOTES
addslashes
strip_tags alone
urlencode for everything
questions.explain: Filter input with a whitelist of allowed characters and use type hints or casting. Escape HTML output with htmlentities and ENT_QUOTES, and use JavaScript Unicode escapes in JavaScript contexts.

questions.q: Besides the general DOM-based vulnerability defenses, what is the key measure for preventing DOM XSS?
choices: Avoid letting data from any untrusted source be written dynamically to the HTML document
Disable JavaScript on all pages
Store all user input in the database before displaying it
Use only GET requests
questions.explain: The main rule is to avoid dynamically writing data from any untrusted source to the HTML document.
